title: Theory and applications of robust optimization
contribution: Survey (first version 2008, arXiv 2010, SIAM Review 2011; read as arXiv 1010.5445v1) that organizes robust optimization around tractability, via duality of the inner problem (nominal class x uncertainty-set class -> counterpart class), together with a priori probability guarantees, risk-measure connections, affine and finite adaptability and an applications map, and names three open problems: tractable adaptable RO, a theory of the price of robustness, and data-driven RO.
problem_entry: Survey stance, not one problem: optimal solutions are fragile to data perturbations; RO is set-based, distinct from robust control and stochastic optimization, and computational tractability is a primary motivation that shaped the field; the entry example is an NP-hard loss-probability portfolio problem (arXiv pp. 2-4). Domains RO CP IO ML AP.
key_idea: The tractability of a robust problem is decided by its inner maximization over U (X(U) convex with an efficient separation test); results are arranged as problem class x set class -> counterpart class, with the budget of uncertainty as the common knob; worst-case solutions need not be overly conservative (arXiv pp. 3, 10-16).
assumptions: Constraint-wise uncertainty in closed sets with stated WLOG reductions (epigraph, projection, singleton sets); tractable = polynomial-time reformulation (footnote 1); Slater condition; guarantees assume independent, symmetric, bounded coefficients or known mean and covariance only; data: 300 monthly returns of 10 equity and debt indices from 1981 (arXiv pp. 3, 5, 9-10, 17).
proof_devices: LP duality of the inner maximization with x fixed: polyhedral set -> LP counterpart of polynomial size (arXiv pp. 10-12)
ellipsoidal set -> SOCP (Theorem 1, Ben-Tal-Nemirovski, arXiv p. 11); general norm set -> dual-norm constraint, l1 and l-infinity give LPs, l2 an SOCP (Theorem 2, arXiv p. 13)
cardinality-constrained (Gamma) set: the natural convex relaxation of the nonconvex set selection is exact, then dualize to an LP (arXiv p. 12)
S-lemma hidden convexity: a robust quadratic constraint under one ellipsoid becomes an LMI/SDP; polyhedral or ellipsoid-intersection sets are NP-hard (Theorem 3, arXiv pp. 13-14)
robust 0-1 problems with Gamma deviating cost coefficients solved by n+1 nominal problems, a logarithmic number for network flows (arXiv pp. 15-16)
a priori violation bounds: 1 - exp(-Omega^2/2) for ellipsoids, exp(-Gamma^2/(2|J|)) for the Gamma-set (Theorem 4), 1/(1+Delta^2) with mean and covariance only (arXiv p. 17)
coherent risk measure <-> uncertainty set conv{E_Q[a]}; CVaR gives a polytope and hence an LP (arXiv pp. 18-19)

two-stage NP-hardness through an indefinite quadratic (example 4.12); affinely adjustable counterpart as a conic program, an LP over the orthant, under fixed recourse (Theorem 5); SDP approximation with a tightness factor under non-fixed recourse (Theorems 6-7) (arXiv pp. 24-27)
finite adaptability: optimal 2-partition NP-hard but efficient in low dimension; static robust solution within a factor of two of the fully adaptable one under symmetry (arXiv pp. 21-22, 28-29)
experiments: One original experiment: 10-asset portfolio, 300 monthly returns from 1981; 600 RO problems (ellipsoid SOCP, D-norm and tail-average LPs) against the exact stochastic program formulated as a MIP at 8 return levels; MOSEK in Matlab on a 2.13 GHz, 2 GB laptop, no solver version; the exact program wins by at most 2-3% in loss probability but needs up to 2.1 h per instance (about 5.2 h for 8) against under 10 min for all 600 RO problems; under 1%, 2% (and 5%) perturbations the exact solutions degrade most and the D-norm set least; admitted to be one random trial (arXiv pp. 5-7). Also summarizes others' computational results, including a negative one (arXiv p. 35).
positioning: Credits Ben-Tal-Nemirovski, El Ghaoui et al. and fast interior-point SDP methods for the field's rise; a condensed complement to the Ben-Tal-El Ghaoui-Nemirovski book plus applications; distinct from sensitivity analysis and robust control; robust dynamic programming criticized for relying on rectangularity; 16 of 136 references carry Bertsimas's name and 11 Caramanis's (arXiv pp. 2, 4, 9, 23, 44-50).
writing: Theme order tractability -> probability -> adaptability -> applications; main message framed as a perhaps surprising implication; moderate personal hedging; an intuition sentence after theorems; the shared term budget of uncertainty used across set families; specific, self-critical future directions (arXiv pp. 3, 7, 11-13, 43-44).
limits_future: Robust counterparts of general convex problems and robust SDPs are intractable; most adaptable RO problems remain intractable; price-of-robustness studies largely empirical; most RO models not connected to data; future: tractable adaptable RO, theoretical bounds on when robustness is cheap or expensive, data-driven RO; not stated: the motivating experiment is one random trial on one data set (arXiv pp. 5-7, 10, 15, 43-44).

method_links.note: Catalogue of class-keeping devices (polyhedral -> LP, ellipsoid -> SOCP, Gamma-set -> LP, norm -> dual norm, robust 0-1 cost uncertainty -> n+1 nominal solves) printed next to the NP-hard boundary (quadratic constraints with polyhedral or ellipsoid-intersection sets, robust SDP, two-stage problems). Tractable is defined by polynomial time while the example argues from measured solve times (the C2 drift).

The budget-of-uncertainty knob trades robustness against performance with a priori probability bounds; but the survey lists the theory of the price of robustness as open because the existing studies, Bertsimas-Sim included, were largely empirical: the probability side was proved, the cost side was not.

Inverted duel: the exact, solver-certified MIP (the stochastic program) is the slow incumbent and the tractable robust approximations are the challengers; exactness wins slightly under the nominal model and loses under perturbation.
A why-now argument is given (late-1990s theory plus fast interior-point methods) but it is not quantified.

Survey written with two earlier co-authors (Caramanis's 2006 MIT dissertation is ref. [52]); the reference list maps the RO cohort ([23]-[36]); future direction 3, data-driven RO, names the programme's next step.

The co-authored text presents Tikhonov-regularized least squares, the Lasso and norm-regularized SVMs as solutions of robust problems: robustifying gives regularity, and sparsity is a consequence of robustness.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Robust and exact solutions re-evaluated under 1%, 2% and 5% perturbations of the return model; the exact stochastic solution degrades most, the D-norm set least. Recurs in S006 (pp. 5, 7) and S086 (pp. 10-14).

transferable: Open a survey with one runnable example that shows the field's central trade-offs and the cost of the exact alternative (arXiv pp. 4-8).
Organize results as nominal class x uncertainty-set class -> counterpart class, marking the NP-hard cells (arXiv pp. 10-16).
Fix x, dualize the inner maximization of a robust constraint and substitute the dual; the counterpart inherits the class of the dual (arXiv pp. 10-12).
For a cardinality-type set, check whether the natural convex relaxation of the inner selection problem is exact before declaring the counterpart nonconvex (arXiv p. 12).
State the a priori violation bound as a function of the knob (exp(-Gamma^2/(2|J|))) so the knob can be set from a target probability (arXiv p. 17).
Print the exact method's solve times on the quality frontier and re-run all methods under 1-5% perturbations of the data (arXiv pp. 6-7).
Close a survey with numbered open problems, including admissions about the field's own evidence base (arXiv pp. 43-44).

quotes.text: computational tractability is also a primary motivation and goal. It is this latter objective that has largely influenced the theoretical trajectory of Robust Optimization
These studies, however, have been largely empirical. Of interest are theoretical bounds to gain an understanding of when robustness is cheap or expensive.

title: The price of fairness
contribution: Defines the price of fairness (the relative loss in total utility of a fair allocation against the utilitarian one) and proves bounds that depend only on the number of players, 1 - (2 sqrt(n) - 1)/n for proportional fairness and 1 - 4n/(n+1)^2 for max-min fairness, uniformly over compact convex utility sets and tight on standard bandwidth examples, with an extension to unequal maximum utilities and a nonconvex example where the price approaches 1.
problem_entry: An implementation failure: FAA air-traffic optimization proposals that cut delay costs remain unimplemented because some airlines would lose relative to the status quo; fairness had axioms but little quantitative trade-off analysis; restated as bounding the price of proportional and max-min fairness (pp. 1-2, 4). Domains AP CP.
key_idea: Abstract the allocation into its utility set and bound the utilitarian optimum through one supporting hyperplane at the fair point (the PF first-order condition; the MMF max-min level on the boundary), which yields a knapsack LP whose value depends only on n (pp. 3, 7-10).
assumptions: Central decision maker with complete information and absolute control; static one-shot allocation; no strategic misreporting; efficiency = sum of utilities; utility set compact and convex (justified by randomization and concave utilities, with primitive sufficient conditions in Proposition 1); equal maximum utilities in Theorem 1, relaxed by scaling in Theorem 2; no data (pp. 3-4, 6-7, 11).
proof_devices: WLOG normalization of the maximum utilities and WLOG monotone utility set, because every scheme considered picks Pareto points (p. 7)
PF first-order optimality condition read as a supporting hyperplane with beta_j = 1/(n u_j^PF) and 1/n <= beta_j <= 1 (eqs. 6-8, p. 8)
utilitarian optimum bounded by the LP relaxation of a knapsack with closed-form value, cited from Bertsimas-Tsitsiklis 1997 (eqs. 9-13, p. 8)
reduction to a two-variable infimum F2 = (2 sqrt(n) - 1)/n by a convex-optimization argument (p. 9)
MMF: max-min level lambda on the ray re, supporting-hyperplane theorem, nonnegativity of the normal via monotonicity, n lambda/(n + 1 - 1/lambda) >= 4n/(n+1)^2 (pp. 9-10)
scale invariance of PF and MMF to extend the bounds to unequal maximum utilities (Theorem 2, pp. 11-12)
tightness on line-graph bandwidth networks: n = 2k - 1 flows for MMF, n = k^2 for PF (pp. 12-14)
three-point nonconvex utility set whose price is arbitrarily close to 1 already for n = 2 (p. 14)
experiments: None computational: the bound tabulated for n = 2-5 (PF 0.086 to 0.306, MMF 0.111 to 0.444) and plotted for n <= 20, plus exact tight examples; one failure reported: PF tightness with unequal maxima not established; real ATFM evaluation announced as under way (pp. 11-14).
positioning: Network fairness studies called typically numerical; Chakrabarty et al.'s polymatroid condition somewhat restrictive; approximate-fairness notions criticized (averaging gives factor-3 approximations that might not be Pareto); price of anarchy set apart; foundations in Nash, Kalai-Smorodinsky, Rawls, Young; claims to be the first of its kind and a theoretical basis for prior empirical work; 6 of 43 references self-citations; the price of robustness is not cited (pp. 2-5, 11, 14-15).
writing: Opens with the FAA and a $10 billion figure; numbered plain-language contributions; axioms glossed one by one; bullet remarks with numbers and an exclamation mark after the theorem; tightness announced as surprising; ethical framing in the conclusion; explicit admission of what could not be established (pp. 1-2, 5, 11-12, 14).
limits_future: Convexity required (otherwise the price approaches 1); PF tightness with unequal maxima open; static model; future: special families of utility sets with smaller prices that are relevant to practice (polymatroids perhaps too narrow) and real ATFM instances (pp. 3, 14).

method_links.note: The paper SKILL.md cites under Method 3: property and stakeholders named, a solution-independent bound uniform over compact convex utility sets, the curve against n with a table, the bad case published (nonconvex sets), tightness on the network community's standard examples.
No continuous knob: the decision maker chooses between two schemes, and the bound's single parameter is the number of players; S026 adds the one-parameter knob alpha.
Structure read off the dual (the PF optimality condition as a supporting hyperplane; the knapsack LP from the LP textbook), but to bound a price, not to build a formulation for a solver.

The owner's problem (FAA, airlines) motivates the paper, but no current rule is evaluated and the real-instance study is deferred; fairness is framed as the condition for implementation, relevant to Method 5's stakeholder correction.
A fairness cohort around one student (Trichakis) and a co-adviser (Farias), with sibling working papers on ATFM and multi-account portfolios.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Starts from efficient ATFM proposals left unimplemented for lack of fairness and prices the property whose absence blocks adoption; recurs in S026 (pp. 11-12).

transferable: Turn the question of why the optimal solution is not implemented into the question of what the property the stakeholders demand costs (p. 1).
Bound the efficient optimum through one supporting hyperplane of the outcome set at the fair point plus a knapsack LP (p. 8).
Pair a structural assumption with a sufficient-condition proposition and a counterexample without it (pp. 7, 14).
Take the outcome set monotone WLOG when every scheme under study selects Pareto points (p. 7).
Prove tightness on the application community's canonical topology (line-graph networks), not on a pathological construction (pp. 12-14).
Follow a worst-case theorem with a small-n table, a plot against n and a managerial reading (p. 11).

quotes.text: the vast majority of these proposals remain unimplemented. The ostensible reason for this is fairness
It is our belief that the “price” of fairness is effectively inescapable if the allocations prescribed by a given scheme are to be ethically acceptable and implementable.

title: Adaptive robust optimization for the security constrained unit commitment problem
contribution: A two-stage adaptive robust security-constrained unit commitment with budgeted nodal net-injection uncertainty, solved by Benders cuts with an outer-approximation inner loop and tested on the ISO New England system against the operator's reserve-adjustment practice: lower average and much less volatile costs and robustness to the load distribution, at 6.14 h against 1.65 h of computing time.
problem_entry: An application change (wind, solar, price-responsive demand) exposes both incumbents: the industry's reserve adjustment with ad hoc reserve rules and capacity shortfalls, and stochastic UC that needs distributions and many scenarios; posed as a two-stage adaptive robust SCUC (pp. 1-3). Domains RO IO AP.
key_idea: Commitment robust to all injections in a budgeted polyhedral set, with a fully adaptive dispatch whose form is set implicitly by the optimization (not affine); the min-max-min model is recast via dispatch duality as a bilinear worst case and solved by an outer Benders loop (MIP master) and an inner outer-approximation loop (pp. 2-5).
assumptions: Binary commitment over 24 h; continuous dispatch, reserves and flows; linear costs with piecewise-linear convex supply curves (admitted as a common assumption); a per-period budgeted set from the nominal singleton to the full box; feasibility via penalty slacks; generator outages and correlations not modelled; ISO-NE data: 312 units, 174 loads, 2,816 nodes, one winter day (pp. 2-5, 9-11).
proof_devices: dualize the dispatch LP to turn the inner max-min into a bilinear program over two polyhedra (eqs. 8-9, p. 3)
worst-case cost R(x) convex piecewise linear as a maximum over extreme points, yet NP-hard to evaluate (eq. 10, p. 4)
outer Benders cutting-plane loop with a MIP master, accelerated by adding dispatch constraints to the master (p. 4)
inner outer approximation (Duran-Grossmann; Fletcher-Leyffer) linearizing the bilinear term; local optimum only, checked by multiple initial conditions (p. 4)
Theorem 1: the cuts are valid because the OA dual solutions are extreme points of the dual polytope (p. 5)
tested alternative: MIO linearization of the bilinear term, with slow convergence at scale (p. 9)
experiments: ISO-NE system with winter-day day-ahead data; baseline reserve adjustment given the same budget knob; 2 x 1,000 simulated loads (uniform; normal, including samples outside the set); $5,000/MWh penalties; GAMS + CPLEX 12.1.0 on a laptop; 6.14 h against 1.65 h (1.46 h with looser tolerances at +0.17% worst-case cost; 8.21 h with 1,876 transmission constraints); dispatch savings up to 2.7%, 1.86-6.96% with a CLT-chosen budget; standard deviation 8.15-14.48 times lower; cross-distribution cost gap 0.037-0.092% against 1.0-2.2%; at 20% variation savings of 12.3% (dispatch) and 9.8% (total); at that level the relative std difference between distributions is not better (43.5-47.7% against 21.78-47.53%) (pp. 5-9).
positioning: Two prior groups (reserve requirements; stochastic UC); hybrid and uncertainty-quantification work presented as compatible; RO lineage including the Bertsimas-Sim budget; concurrent robust-UC reports criticized (no reserves, no efficiency or stability study) with an independence statement; affine policies contrasted; MINLP outer approximation borrowed; 3 of 28 references self-citations (pp. 1-3, 11).
writing: Numbered contributions; conclusions a)-d) before the evidence; an explicit myth correction (robust optimization is not always conservative); dollar savings per day; benefit-risk tables for decision makers; operational placement in the reliability UC phase; strong adjectives and an abstract claim of robustness to all realizations despite local inner solves (pp. 1-2, 4, 6-7, 9).
limits_future: Local inner optimum; slower run time; linear costs, with nonconvex costs needing a modified OA; slow MIO linearization; no outages or correlations; future: re-commitment with updated forecasts, price volatility, correlated sets, affine dispatch rules, outage uncertainty, impact on reserves; not stated: one test day, no worst-case certificate, simulation only (pp. 4-5, 9-10).

method_links.note: Partner co-authors (three ISO-NE staff) supply the system, the data and the baseline, which is the operator's current reserve-adjustment practice; decisions scored by simulated dispatch and total cost, volatility and penalties; the method's own slower run time reported (6.14 h against 1.65 h); no field test, the model placed in the reliability UC phase.

The budget is the knob and benefit-risk tables go to decision makers; with the budget set by the central limit theorem the price is negative (the robust plan is cheaper on average); no solution-independent bound; the knob is calibrated by a limit law, neither from data nor arbitrarily.
The adaptive model leaves the MIP class (a bilinear, NP-hard inner max-min); the paper changes the solution device (Benders + OA), not the formulation, and measures solve times at the target scale.
No certificate for the worst case (the OA local optimum is checked only by restarts) while the abstract calls the solutions robust against all realizations; an instance of Tension T1.
Negative results printed in the body: the slower run time and the slow MIO linearization.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The uncertainty budget is chosen by the central-limit scaling of aggregated independent loads rather than the worst case, giving the largest savings; compare S003's a priori bound exp(-Gamma^2/(2|J|)) (S003 arXiv p. 17).
Commitments evaluated on loads from two distributions, normal samples falling outside the budgeted set; recurs in S003 (arXiv pp. 6-7) and S086 (pp. 10-14).

The incumbent reserve rule receives the same uncertainty budget (reserve adjustment proportional to total load variation) and both are compared over the whole knob range; close to Method 4 step 5 (matched complexity); compare S086 p. 9.

transferable: Name both incumbents (the industry rule and the academic alternative) and one concrete failure of each (pp. 1-2).
Keep the industry rule for the risks the uncertainty set does not model and replace only its ad hoc part (p. 9).
Write the worst-case recourse as a maximum over extreme points of the dual polytope so that cuts from locally solved inner problems stay valid (pp. 4-5).
Try the textbook MIO linearization of the bilinear subproblem and report it when it is slower (p. 9).
Give the incumbent rule the same conservatism knob and compare the two across the knob's whole range (p. 5).
Evaluate decisions under two load distributions, including out-of-set samples, and report the cross-distribution difference as a robustness metric (pp. 5, 7).
Report your own run time next to the baseline's, together with the quality cost of looser tolerances (pp. 5-6).
Calibrate the budget by the central-limit scaling of aggregated independent uncertainties (p. 6).
coauthors: Eugene Litvinov, Xu Andy Sun, Jinye Zhao, Tongxin Zheng

quotes.text: We want to remark that point a) is quite contrary to the general impression that robust optimization is always conservative.
This demonstrates that we can choose a proper uncertainty level by using the probability law as a guideline as opposed to always hedging against the most extreme scenarios.

title: On the efficiency-fairness trade-off
contribution: Reduces the design of a fair operational objective to choosing alpha in the alpha-fair welfare family, gives instance-free worst-case curves for the efficiency lost (price of fairness, 1 - Theta(n^(-alpha/(alpha+1)))) and the fairness lost (price of efficiency, 1 - Theta(n^(-1/alpha))), turns them into managerial rules for picking alpha, and tests them on four airlines' historical air-traffic data against ration-by-schedule.
problem_entry: Managers design objectives for resource allocation (call centres, healthcare, ATFM, organ allocation) in an ad hoc way; utilitarian objectives ignore inequity when compensation is impossible; problem: choose the inequality-aversion parameter alpha using worst-case efficiency and fairness losses (pp. 1-2, 7-10). Domains AP CP.
key_idea: The alpha-fair (Atkinson constant-elasticity) family nests utilitarian, proportional and max-min fairness, so one knob spans the debate; two instance-free trade-off curves (price of fairness, price of efficiency) parametrized by alpha guide its choice; the minimum utility is the fairness metric because it alone keeps max-min fairness optimal (pp. 2, 6-10).
assumptions: The S012 framework: central decision maker, utility set compact and convex (randomization for nonconvex sets), equal maximum utilities (a general bound with ratio B/L otherwise), no cash transfers, efficiency = utilitarian sum; case study: the Bertsimas-Stock-Patterson ATFM integer model, airborne delay weighted 1.5, utilities = delay reduction against RBS, 4 airlines, 54 airports, about 4,000 flights, 2 severe-weather days; the convexity of the ATFM utility set is not discussed (pp. 2, 5-8, 12-14).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: price-of-fairness bound as 1 minus a one-dimensional minimum over x in [1, n], read as 1 - Theta(n^(-alpha/(alpha+1))) through garbled glyphs (p. 7)
unimodality of the bound's objective (online appendix C, not read), so the exact bound is computable (p. 7)
unequal-maxima bound (2) depending on the ratio B/L (p. 8)
near-worst-case constructions: line-graph networks and a single resource with two consumption rates; average gap 0.005, maximum 0.023 (pp. 8-9)
Theorem 2: price-of-efficiency bound 1 - Theta(n^(-1/alpha)) with a root condition, tight on a single-resource example (p. 10)
fairness metric chosen by a requirement (max-min fairness optimal among Pareto allocations), with a two-point counterexample for the other inequality indices (footnote 2, p. 9)
experiments: ATFM case on two severe-weather days, 4 airlines, utilitarian against alpha = 0.5, 1, 2 and max-min, for flight and passenger delay; the utilitarian plan cuts delay by about 10% against RBS but leaves some airlines with no gain; alpha = 2 gives a price of fairness of about 7.6% and a price of efficiency of about 3.8% (an instance-specific alpha = 1 would give 6.5% and 7.7%); a 20% tolerance rule was conservative for flight delays (actual loss 5%) but not for passenger delays (about 15%); assumption checked through coefficients of variation 0.015 and 0.007; no solver, run times or gaps reported (pp. 13-16).
positioning: Welfare-economics and bargaining foundations; application survey (healthcare, services, ATFM, networks); the group's own ATFM fairness notions called ad hoc; S012 reconstructed by a unified geometric framework; claims the first general characterizations of these trade-off curves; links to achievable-performance spaces (Bertsimas-Paschalidis-Tsitsiklis 1994); 6 of 50 references self-citations (pp. 2-6, 12, 16-17).
writing: Opens with a question and four examples; managerial merits in bullets; prescriptions as rules for a manager with four parties and a 20% tolerance; a principled-versus-ad-hoc contrast; an exclamation mark at a 100% price of efficiency; takeaways headed Quality of Decisions and Robustness Matters; hedges such as near-tight and potential managerial implications (pp. 1, 3, 8, 10-11, 15).
limits_future: The worst case can be conservative on an instance; unequal maxima weaken the bounds; the choice of fairness metric is nebulous; future: use problem invariants to constrain the utility set and compute curves; not stated: proofs outside the article, two days and four airlines, no computational report, and an internal inconsistency in the alpha for the 20% rule (about 1 on p. 11, about 0.5 on p. 16) (pp. 8-9, 11, 15-16).

method_links.note: Strong: property and owners named, one interpretable knob alpha, solution-independent worst-case bounds in both directions, curves and decision rules handed to the manager, a real case plus the case where the worst case proves conservative; it also bounds the price itself, the open problem S003 named for robustness (S003 arXiv p. 43).

On Method 3's correction to set the knob from data: the paper argues for an instance-free, worst-case choice of alpha, because data-calibrated curves depend on which historical instances are chosen, which is likely to create tension between airlines, and may be brittle to unprecedented shocks; computed curves only when extra invariants are known.

Owner FAA; the current rule RBS (considered fair) is the zero point of each airline's utility; real historical data; decision metric = delay reduction per airline; no field test, and the optimization proposals remain unimplemented.
The fairness line continues with the same student and co-adviser, a kidney-allocation paper and the group's ATFM fairness papers.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: ATFM optimization proposals promise about 10% less delay but are not implemented because the gains are not split equitably; the paper designs the objective for adoption; with S012 (p. 1).

A one-parameter axiomatic family contains the incumbent objectives (utilitarian, proportional, max-min) as special cases and reconstructs the authors' earlier bounds; compare S086 Proposition 2(b) (p. 5).

transferable: Recast the choice of an objective as the choice of one parameter in an axiomatically grounded family (p. 2).
Define a price in each direction (efficiency lost to fairness, fairness lost to efficiency) and plot them against each other, parametrized by the knob (pp. 7, 10-11).
Choose the evaluation metric by a requirement and show with a two-point counterexample that the standard indices fail it (p. 9).
Measure each stakeholder's utility as improvement over the current rule, so the status quo is the zero point (pp. 12-13).
Prove the bound's one-dimensional objective unimodal so practitioners can compute the exact bound for their n and knob (p. 7).
Check the theorem's assumption on the real data (coefficients of variation of the maximum utilities) and switch to the general bound when it fails (p. 14).
Turn worst-case curves into two decision rules (a tolerance; a balance of the two prices) and a sweet-spot range for the knob (pp. 10-11).
Test an instance-free prescription on real instances and report what an instance-specific choice would have gained and when the worst case was conservative (pp. 15-16).

quotes.text: This crucial design task is nonetheless frequently executed in an ad hoc fashion.
the worst-case analysis is an instance-free approach, better suited for decisions in such an environment.

title: Inverse optimization: A new perspective on the Black-Litterman model
contribution: Shows that the Black-Litterman estimator is the solution of a convex inverse-optimization problem (an LMI/SDP built from the optimality conditions of the investors' forward problem, with views as constraints and minimal-norm violation), generalizes it to volatility views, factor structure and coherent risk measures through robust optimization and conic duality, and proposes MV-IO and RMV-IO estimators that take less risk and are more robust to wrong views than BL in simulations and an MSCI-sector backtest.
problem_entry: The industry-standard Black-Litterman model allows views only on returns and rests on mean-variance; statistical extensions are often nonconvex and reverse optimization is ad hoc for constrained problems; problem: characterize BL as the solution of a convex inverse-optimization problem and generalize it (pp. 1-2). Domains CP RO AP.
key_idea: Replace BL's statistical framework with inverse optimization: the KKT conditions of the forward problem with the data as unknowns give an LMI that treats mean and covariance on the same footing; views as constraints with a minimal-norm perturbation give an SDP that recovers BL when the covariance is fixed, then extends to volatility views, factor models and coherent risk through a robust forward problem (pp. 1, 5-9).
assumptions: Markowitz with risk-free lending and borrowing; a CAPM-type equilibrium with investor-specific risk thresholds; Sigma positive definite and L > 0; a conic-representable uncertainty set with an interior point and a unique optimum; Gaussian returns only for the VaR and CVaR equivalences; RMV-IO needs a priori parameters and an exogenous scale z matched to BL for comparison; data: 10 MSCI sector indices (DataStream, WRDS), 24 months to May 1998; backtest June 1992 to December 2009 (pp. 2-3, 5, 7-9, 12, 14).
proof_devices: KKT conditions, necessary and sufficient under Slater, define the inverse feasible set (Proposition 1, p. 5)
change of variables Sigma_bar = 2 delta Sigma makes the equilibrium system an LMI (Theorem 1, p. 5)
Schur complement -> SDP; the least-squares closed form recovers the BL update when Sigma is fixed (Proposition 2, p. 5)
closed-form minimum of a linear function over an ellipsoid gives the Markowitz, VaR and CVaR equivalences; coherent risk measures <-> convex uncertainty sets (Propositions 3-4, p. 7)
scaling and aggregation over investors show that the market portfolio is optimal for some L* (Propositions 5-6, pp. 7-8)
double conic duality: dualize the inner minimization over the uncertainty set, dualize again, and write primal-dual optimality as a conic system in the unknown data (Theorem 2, p. 8)
experiments: Aim stated as finding when and how to use the flexibility, not a winner; matched comparison (return views only, factor-structured covariance for BL, repeated with the full and a rank-3 covariance); simulations of view accuracy, rising confidence in wrong views, covariance perturbation (10,000 simulations) and a view in the factor space; backtest on MSCI sectors monthly from June 1998, target std 15.73%, a Markowitz comparator, a static view, systematic-bias views and a 72-month window check; IO portfolios take up to 6% (overall) and 11% (maximum) less std; BL wins with accurate views; return conclusions depend on the window; CVX (pp. 9-14).
positioning: BL literature and its statistical extensions; inverse-optimization lineage (Heuberger, Ahuja-Orlin, Iyengar-Kang); reverse optimization called ad hoc; claims the first rigorous inverse-optimization interpretation of BL, unifying several threads; re-derives Herold's results as a special case; an endnote corrects the record on the Bayesian interpretation; 3 of 35 references self-citations, including S003 (pp. 1-2, 6, 14-15).
writing: A key-insight sentence in the abstract and the introduction; one running 10-sector table with a column per estimator; numbered contributions; key insights before the experiments; an explicit warning against over-reading window-dependent results; a hedged conclusion (pp. 1-2, 4-10, 12, 14).
limits_future: The general RMV-IO system cannot be solved without fixing parameters; exogenous scale parameters; BL better with accurate views; no gain for views in the factor space; window-dependent inferences; future: shrinkage-based and data-driven CVaR IO estimators, properties under view-generation mechanisms; not stated: one static view, 10 sectors, no transaction costs (pp. 9, 12-14).

method_links.note: A model owned by another tradition (the statistical, Bayesian BL estimator used in industry) is rewritten exactly as a convex LMI/SDP problem that recovers the original as a special case; the structure is read off KKT and conic duality.

An inverse rather than a robust problem: BL works well in practice, so the authors find the optimization problem it solves exactly and extend it from there; the robust problem enters only in the extension (19).

A duel against the incumbent at matched complexity (factor-structured BL covariance, return views only) with a report of where the method wins (risk control, wrong or uncertain views) and where it loses (accurate views), but with no MIO, warm start or certificate.

The incumbent is the industry's standard estimator, not a partner's current rule; decisions scored by return, risk and Sharpe ratio in simulation and backtest; no partner or field test; industry funding (Citigroup) disclosed.
Inverse optimization presented as a research programme across fields, carried by a PhD student.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Proposition 2(b): with the covariance fixed, the inverse-optimization estimate equals BL's; the restriction is then relaxed to add volatility views and new risk measures; compare S026 (pp. 4, 6).
Wrong views held with rising confidence, a perturbed covariance and shifted backtest windows; compare S003 (arXiv pp. 6-7) and S006 (pp. 5, 7).

transferable: Ask which optimization problem an industry heuristic solves exactly (p. 2).
Inverse-optimization recipe: forward problem -> optimality conditions with the data as unknowns -> views as constraints -> smallest-norm perturbation (pp. 5-6).
Change variables so that the inverse system is linear in the data, then use a Schur complement to get an SDP (p. 5).
Invert a robust forward problem by double conic duality (p. 8).
Fix unidentifiable scale parameters at the incumbent's values so the comparison isolates the new idea (p. 9).
Give the baseline the new method's structural ingredient, then repeat with its native setting (pp. 9, 14).
Separate input accuracy from model assumptions with stylized simulations before a backtest, and rerun the backtest on a shifted window before claiming a winner (pp. 9-13).
Carry one running example table with a column per new estimator through the paper (pp. 4-9).

quotes.text: The key insight is to replace the statistical framework in the original approach with ideas from inverse optimization.
The role of numerical testing, then, is not to decide which procedure “outperforms” the other, but rather to help identify when and how to use this additional flexibility.
